q: Name a programming language that first appeared before 1980.

answers.l: Dennis Ritchie, Bell Labs, 1972. It grew up alongside Unix.
John Backus’s team at IBM, 1957. Skeptics doubted a compiler could match hand-written assembly. It came close.
1959, by the CODASYL committee, drawing heavily on Grace Hopper’s FLOW-MATIC. Still moves much of the world’s money.
John McCarthy, 1958. Brought garbage collection, conditional expressions and the REPL.
Kemeny and Kurtz, Dartmouth, 1964. Built for time-sharing so every student could program.
Niklaus Wirth, 1970. Designed to teach structured programming.
IBM, 1974, as SEQUEL. Renamed because an aircraft company held the trademark.
Xerox PARC in the 1970s: Alan Kay, Dan Ingalls, Adele Goldberg. Everything is an object, even classes.
Colmerauer and Roussel, Marseille, 1972. Programs are facts and rules; the runtime searches for proofs.
The ALGOL 60 report introduced Backus–Naur form. Most later languages descend from it.
Steele and Sussman, MIT, 1975. Lexical scope and proper tail calls in a tiny Lisp.
Dahl and Nygaard, Oslo. Simula 67 introduced classes, objects and inheritance.
Robin Milner, Edinburgh, 1973. The metalanguage of the LCF prover, and home of Hindley–Milner type inference.
Kenneth Iverson’s 1962 notation became a language. It needed its own keyboard.
Chuck Moore, around 1970. Stack-based, and an early workhorse for telescope control.
Ken Thompson, around 1969. Kernighan’s B tutorial contains the earliest known "hello, world".
Martin Richards, 1967. The ancestor of B, and so of C.
Aho, Weinberger and Kernighan, 1977. Named after their initials.
Feurzeig, Papert and Solomon, 1967. Taught a generation to steer a turtle.
IBM, 1964. An attempt to replace FORTRAN and COBOL at once.
Barbara Liskov’s group at MIT, 1974. Iterators and abstract data types.
Massachusetts General Hospital, 1966. Still runs major health-record systems.
IBM’s Report Program Generator, 1959. Still in production on IBM i.
Bell Labs, 1962. String pattern matching before regex went mainstream.
Wirth again, 1978. Pascal with modules.
Cleve Moler wrote the original in the late 1970s so students could use LINPACK without writing Fortran.
Grace Hopper’s team, 1955 onward. English-like and the main ancestor of COBOL.
Lee McMahon, Bell Labs, 1974. A stream editor that is also a small language.
MIT’s Lisp of the 1960s and 70s. Ancestor of Common Lisp.
Xerox PARC, 1976. Gave us "Mesa semantics" for condition variables, which Java and most others use.
Ralph Griswold, 1977. SNOBOL’s successor, built on goal-directed evaluation.
"Jules’ Own Version of the International Algebraic Language," 1959. Flew in US Air Force avionics for decades.
Konrad Zuse designed it in the 1940s. The first high-level language design, implemented decades later.
Information Processing Language, 1956. Newell, Shaw and Simon. It introduced list processing.
John Backus, 1953, for the IBM 701. Floating point by interpreter, before FORTRAN.
Proposed by John Mauchly in 1949. Interpreted on UNIVAC, about 50 times slower than machine code.
Alick Glennie, 1952, for the Manchester Mark 1. Often called the first compiled language.
Grace Hopper, 1952. The A-0 System is often called the first compiler, though it worked more like a linker.
RAND, 1963. One of the first interactive, time-shared languages.
Kernighan, 1974. "Rational Fortran," a preprocessor that gave Fortran C-like control flow.
Bjarne Stroustrup’s 1979 project. It was renamed C++ in 1983.

nope.ada: Standardized in 1980 as MIL-STD-1815, after Lovelace’s birth year. Missed by months.
nope.c++: Named C++ in 1983. Its 1979 ancestor, C with Classes, would count.
nope.python: 1991. Guido started it over Christmas 1989, still too late.

traps.q: Name the language Dennis Ritchie created at Bell Labs as the successor to B.
Name the language whose name abbreviates "FORmula TRANslation."
